I asked claude if any papers have shown helicase activity - what do you think? I can curate the paper since it's been published if you think it is worth saying that it is not a helicase:

Short answer: No. As far as the published literature goes, no paper has biochemically demonstrated helicase (ATP-dependent RNA unwinding) activity for the Yb protein itself. The "helicase" label is based on sequence/structural prediction, not enzymology.
The details:
The Yb protein is routinely annotated as a Tudor-domain RNA helicase or a DEAD-box-like RNA helicase, and its central domain does show similarity to DEAD-box helicase cores. Yb's N-terminal RecA-like domain has notable similarity to DEAD-box proteins like Vasa, DDX5, and DDX18, including the Q motif and motifs I, Ia, Ib, II, and III [Cell Reports](https://www.cell.com/article/S2211-1247(14)00437-9/fulltext). But annotation ≠ demonstrated activity.
What has actually been shown experimentally about the helicase domain is RNA binding, not unwinding:

Ishizu et al. (2015, Cell Reports) mutated conserved residues Gln399, Pro455, and Asp537 in Yb's putative helicase motifs and found these abolished RNA binding and Yb-body formation, but the assays were CLIP and pulldown — no ATPase or duplex-unwinding assays were performed.
Hirakata et al. (2019, EMBO Reports) similarly showed that mutating Gln399 or Asp537 in the RNA helicase domain to alanine severely reduced RNA-binding by Yb, and these mutants failed to form Yb bodies or restore piRNA biogenesis [PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6607011/) — again, binding-based assays, not unwinding.

In fact, one early paper explicitly argued against Yb being a true helicase. Szakmary et al. (2009, JCB) noted that Yb's helicase-homologous region does not contain an obvious DEAD-box motif and concluded Yb is unlikely to function as an RNA helicase, though it could have other RNA-related functions [Rockefeller University Press](https://rupress.org/jcb/article/185/4/613/35184/The-Yb-protein-defines-a-novel-organelle-and).
This contrasts sharply with its partner Armitage (Armi), where helicase activity has been directly demonstrated. Pandey et al. (2017, PLOS Genetics) incubated recombinant Armi with RNA duplexes carrying 5′ or 3′ overhangs in the presence or absence of ATP and showed an ATP-dependent unwinding activity specific to 5′-overhang substrates, which was abolished in an ATPase-dead mutant [PLOS](https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1006956). That is the kind of experiment that would be needed to demonstrate helicase activity for Yb — and to my knowledge it has never been done (or at least never published with a positive result).
So if you're writing or reviewing something and the claim is "Yb is an RNA helicase," it's worth softening to "predicted/putative RNA helicase" or "Yb contains a DEAD-box-like helicase domain required for RNA binding" — the unwinding step has not been shown biochemically.
If you've seen a recent paper that contradicts this, I'd be curious to look — but as of what's currently in the literature, the helicase activity of Yb remains an inference from sequence rather than a demonstrated biochemical property.

author: sjm41
body:
Thanks for the extra info @Antonialock - it's very helpful.
I think you and Claude are right - there is some similarity evidence for fs(1)Yb being a helicase, but nothing really convincing, but nothing to prove it's not either.

Curiously, the two paralogs of this gene do have additional evidence for 'helicase activity' via other routes:
- BoYb (Q9VNP5) has Interpro domains 'DEAD/DEAH-box helicase domain' and 'Helicase superfamily 1/2, ATP-binding domain' (though these don't generate GO annotations)
- SoYb (Q9VL52) has InterPro 'RNA helicase, DEAD-box type, Q motif', which generates a 'RNA helicase activity' GO annotation.

So, it seems the evidence for Yb having helicase activity is less than for the other two (especially considering "_Szakmary et al. (2009, JCB) noted that Yb's helicase-homologous region does not contain an obvious DEAD-box motif and concluded Yb is unlikely to function as an RNA helicase_"), but it's not unreasonable for ARBA to predict helicase activity for Yb.

So I think we can leave this one alone and close the ticket (at least, until we have some actual EXP evidence to use).
